q: A new project manager asks where a project's governance comes from. What is the best answer?
explanation: Project governance is shaped by the performing organization's governance model and by stakeholders such as customers and regulators. It applies to predictive, adaptive and hybrid projects.
options: It is invented fresh by each new project team, on its own
From the organization's governance and its stakeholders
It is set only by the project's main contractor
It applies only to predictive projects

q: Halfway through, a project has already delivered the value it was set up for, under budget. The board closes it early. Which governance scenario is this?
options: Early termination for negative cause
Project contraction
Replanning
Early termination for positive cause
explanation: Early termination for positive cause: the project or phase closes before using its planned schedule or budget because the desired value impact has been achieved.

q: An agile team governs itself, but its members' decisions are starting to pull in different directions. What does the PMBOK Guide suggest?
options: Common measurable objectives with leading indicators
Replace it at once with a heavy structured model
Let each member decide alone
Remove all feedback to save time
explanation: A key challenge of self-governance is fragmented decision-making. Clear, measurable common objectives, supported by leading indicators and feedback mechanisms, help self-governed teams align.

q: Which of these is one of the three core components of effective project governance?
options: A large governance board for every project
Detailed daily time sheets for all team members
Signaling mechanisms such as leading indicators
A fixed template for every project report
explanation: Effective governance needs target metrics aligned with strategy, signaling mechanisms for those metrics (typically leading indicators), and feedback mechanisms for decision-makers.

q: A PMO proposes to judge project governance by the percentage of team members who finished a training class. What is the weakness?
explanation: Governance metrics should measure how well projects achieve their target outcomes, not input metrics such as resource utilization, compliance with a set of standards, or training completed.
options: Training should never be measured at all
It measures an input, not an outcome
Percentages cannot be reported to a board
Only the sponsor may set metrics

q: The project uses the company's risk register template and its change control procedure. What are these?
options: Enterprise environmental factors
Project deliverables
Work performance data
Organizational process assets
explanation: Templates and procedures such as change control are organizational process assets in the group 'policies, processes and procedures'.

q: Who updates the organizational knowledge repositories, such as lessons learned and performance metrics, during a project?
options: The project, throughout its life
Only the PMO, after the project has closed
No one, since they are fixed
The external auditors
explanation: Knowledge repositories are updated throughout the project with project information. Policies, processes and procedures, by contrast, are usually set outside the project.

q: The team wants to change the company's standard procurement procedure to suit its project. What applies?
options: The team may change it as it wishes
The sponsor may override it with a quick verbal OK
It changes only through organizational policy
Procedures do not apply to projects
explanation: Policies, processes and procedures are usually established by the PMO or another function and can be updated only by following organizational policies; some organizations allow teams to tailor templates and checklists.

q: A vendor bidding for the project's contract offers the project manager expensive concert tickets. What should the project manager do?
options: Accept, as long as the bid is judged fairly
Decline and follow the gift policy
Accept and share them with the team
Ask the other bidders for similar gifts
explanation: Fairness requires decisions free of competing self-interest; contracts are not awarded based on personal considerations. Following the organization's policies is a mandatory responsibility standard.

q: A firm owned by the project manager's brother-in-law submits a bid. What does the Code require first?
options: Reject the firm's bid at once, without review
Score the bid quietly but fairly
Award it if it is the cheapest
Disclose it and stay out of the decision
explanation: We disclose real or potential conflicts of interest and refrain from the decision until we have made full disclosure, have an approved mitigation plan, and have the stakeholders' consent.

q: The sponsor asks the project manager to leave a two-month delay out of the board report 'until it is fixed'. What should the project manager do?
explanation: Honesty forbids half-truths and withholding information that would make statements misleading. We provide accurate information in a timely manner and share bad news, even when it is poorly received.
options: Report the delay accurately, with a plan
Leave it out, as the sponsor asks
Report only the parts of the work that are on time
Resign from the project at once

q: A team member tells the project manager that a colleague falsified test results. What does the Code require?
options: Ignore it unless a customer complains
Warn the colleague privately and move on
Report it to the appropriate management
Post it in the team's chat channel
explanation: We report unethical or illegal conduct to appropriate management and, if necessary, to those affected; complaints must be substantiated by facts.

q: After raising a safety concern in good faith, an engineer is moved off the team as a punishment. Which part of the Code is broken?
options: Fairness: equal access to information for all
Responsibility: no retaliation for good-faith concerns
Honesty: no half-truths
Respect: respect for property rights
explanation: We do not retaliate against persons for raising good-faith ethical concerns; retaliatory conduct is subject to disciplinary action.

q: Which of these is a mandatory standard of the Code, rather than an aspirational one?
options: We strive to be inclusive leaders
We seek to understand the truth
We listen actively to others
We negotiate in good faith
explanation: Negotiating in good faith is a mandatory respect standard. The others are aspirational: conduct we strive for, not firm requirements subject to discipline.

q: The final report shows the project finished on time and on budget, but customers rarely use the product. How should its success be judged?
options: Project management succeeded; the outcome did not
A full success, since every constraint was met
A full failure, since money was spent
Success cannot be judged after closure
explanation: Success has two dimensions: project management efficiency (cost, scope, time, quality) and project outcomes (realizing the intended value). Here only the first was achieved.

q: Where are the measurable project objectives and related success criteria first recorded?
options: The lessons learned register
The issue log
The project charter
The team charter
explanation: Table 4-1 lists measurable project objectives and related success criteria among the elements of the project charter.

q: A proposed success metric reads: 'Customers should like the new app.' What should the project manager do?
options: Accept it, as satisfaction can never be measured
Make it SMART: a rating target by a date
Replace it with the project's budget
Leave the metrics to the vendor
explanation: Metrics should be specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound, for example an average customer rating to reach by a set date.

q: In which situation does the PMBOK Guide say escalation is especially useful?
options: When the team wants to avoid making decisions
Only in agile, self-governing teams
Whenever a team member disagrees
When authority sits outside the team
explanation: Escalation is useful in hierarchical organizations where decision authority includes people outside the team, or where higher-ranking people can remove persistent obstacles or resolve conflicts.

q: A lender funds a building in stages and, at set points, reviews whether the next round of funding still makes business sense. Which governance component is this?
options: Investment control
Self-governance
Benefits realization
Rolling wave planning
explanation: Investment control gives formal stewardship of funds, often with defined decision points in the design and build phases, as in lender-financed construction.

q: A cost overrun is still within the project manager's agreed control threshold. What should the project manager do?
explanation: Control thresholds set the variance allowed before action outside the project is needed. Within the threshold, the project manager acts and reports as usual.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Financial management plan
options: Escalate it at once to the whole governance board
Hide it until the next phase
Handle it at project level and report it
Ask the team to vote on it

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Financial management plan

q: A change would exceed the project manager's authority. Two board members are friends of the project manager. What should happen?
options: Ask the friends to approve it informally
Take it through the agreed escalation path
Split it into small changes under the limit
Make the change and report it later
explanation: Governance defines roles and decision-making authority; changes beyond the project manager's authority follow the agreed path. Splitting or informal approval would also break the Code's fairness standards.

q: In guided self-governance, what limits an agile team's decisions?
options: The PMO approves every task
Nothing at all, as the team is fully free
Daily approval from the sponsor
Agreed boundaries and guardrails
explanation: Agile teams manage their work with light governance and clearly set boundaries and guardrails, deciding their own processes, priorities and problem-solving approaches.

q: A portfolio board wants a metric showing whether its project prioritization decisions were effective. Which example does the PMBOK Guide give?
options: Return on investment
Hours logged per team member
Number of meetings held
Pages of documentation
explanation: Example governance metrics include indicators of how effective prioritization decisions are, such as ROI; indicators of due-date performance; and whether the baseline carries the highest value.

q: When governance is set up for a project, what should be identified, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Only the end users of the product
The vendors' sales and marketing teams
Control boards, committees and their members
The team members' families
explanation: Tailoring governance requires identifying the control boards, committees and other stakeholders that are part of the project, and defining the status reporting requirements.

q: How does the PMBOK Guide say governance should be tailored to the approach?
options: Comprehensive for adaptive work, light for predictive
Light for adaptive, comprehensive for large predictive
The same weight for every project
None at all for hybrid projects
explanation: Governance can be lightweight for adaptive methods, moderate or combined for hybrid projects, and comprehensive for large predictive portfolios, programs and projects.

q: Which TWO are values of the PMI Code of Ethics and Professional Conduct?
options: Respect
Fairness
Efficiency
Loyalty
Profitability
explanation: The four values are responsibility, respect, fairness and honesty.

q: Which THREE are organizational process assets of the type 'policies, processes and procedures'?
options: Change control procedures
Risk register templates
Preapproved supplier lists
Marketplace conditions
Government regulations
Currency exchange rates
explanation: Change control procedures, templates and preapproved supplier lists are OPAs. Marketplace conditions, regulations and exchange rates are external enterprise environmental factors.

q: Which TWO measure the success of project outcomes rather than of project management?
options: Return on investment achieved
New customers acquired
Delivered within budget
Finished on schedule
Scope delivered as planned
explanation: Outcome success covers strategic objectives such as ROI, new customers, being first to market and sustainability goals. Budget, schedule and scope measure project management efficiency.

q: Match each governance scenario with its description.
right: A plan revision that needs review
Constraints change to keep the value
Closed early, as the value is no longer achievable
explanation: Table 2-2 also lists early termination for positive cause, when the value has already been achieved. In every case, the value proposition is the main factor.

q: Complete each statement about the PMI Code of Ethics.

blanks.text: Disclosing a conflict of interest is part of
Reporting illegal conduct to management is part of
Avoiding half-truths and misleading omissions is part of

explanation: Conflicts of interest are under fairness; reporting violations under responsibility; not deceiving under honesty.
